lesson.title: Shift and Invert: Half-Wave Symmetry and the Missing Even Harmonics
lesson.summary: A waveform has half-wave symmetry when shifting it by half a period exactly inverts it, f(t + T/2) equals negative f(t), and that forces every even-numbered harmonic to vanish, leaving only odd harmonics.
lesson.body:
Even symmetry and odd symmetry are both about comparing a waveform to its own mirror image at a single snapshot in time. Half-wave symmetry is a different kind of test: it compares the waveform to a copy of itself shifted forward by half a period. If that shifted copy turns out to be the exact negative of the original everywhere, f(t + T/2) = -f(t), the waveform has half-wave symmetry. This test is independent of even and odd symmetry; a waveform can have half-wave symmetry alone, combine it with even or odd symmetry, or have none of the three, as the next chapter shows directly.

Here is why half-wave symmetry wipes out every even harmonic. Consider the second harmonic on its own: its own period is exactly T/2, so shifting time by T/2 carries it through exactly one full cycle of itself, and cos(2 omega0 (t + T/2)) = cos(2 omega0 t + 2 pi) = cos(2 omega0 t), unchanged, no sign flip. The same is true for every even harmonic. Now consider the third harmonic: shifting by T/2 carries it through one and a half of its own cycles, and cos(3 omega0 (t + T/2)) = cos(3 omega0 t + 3 pi) = -cos(3 omega0 t), a sign flip. The same sign flip happens for every odd harmonic, and for the DC term a T/2 shift obviously changes nothing, so a0 cannot flip sign either. Since the whole waveform is required to flip sign after a T/2 shift, it can only be built from pieces that themselves flip sign under that shift, the odd harmonics, and it cannot contain any DC term or any even harmonic, since none of those pieces flip.

As a fully worked example, return to the square wave, this time in its usual phase: f(t) = A for 0 < t < T/2, and f(t) = -A for T/2 < t < T. Test the half-wave condition directly: for t between 0 and T/2, t + T/2 falls between T/2 and T, where f equals -A; and -f(t) at that same t is -A as well, since f(t) = A there. They match, so f(t + T/2) = -f(t): half-wave symmetry confirmed. This lines up exactly with the result already verified in the Odd Symmetry chapter, that this square wave's Fourier series contains bn = 4A/(n pi) for odd n only, with every even harmonic and the DC term equal to zero. Half-wave symmetry predicted that outcome in advance, purely from the shape of the wave.

A useful contrast: a full-wave rectified sine wave, f(t) = A|sin(omega0 t)|, is never negative, so it can never satisfy f(t + T/2) = -f(t) unless the signal were zero everywhere, which it is not. It has no half-wave symmetry, and, unlike the square wave, it does contain a nonzero DC term and even harmonics, which the Waveform Symmetry chapter examines directly. Half-wave symmetry also shows up by design in real power electronics: many inverter and motor drive output waveforms are deliberately built with half-wave symmetry specifically so their spectra contain no even harmonics, simplifying the output filter needed to clean them up.
